key_insight: In low-dimensional pnictogen chalcohalides, surface orientation can shift band edges enough to strongly alter charge extraction, making facet control a hidden lever for solar-cell performance.
engineering_relevance: For photovoltaic device design, selecting or engineering stable surface facets and contact alignments may be as important as bulk absorber optimization for improving voltage and efficiency.
method: First-principles calculations sampled many crystal orientations across Bi/Sb chalcogen-halide compounds.
Surface formation energies and band alignments were compared for low-symmetry facets, especially (011) and (010).
Drift-diffusion device modeling tested how mixed surface terminations affect BiSBr solar-cell voltage.
evidence_signal: Across eight compounds, the most stable (011) and (010) facets differed in formation energy by only about 0.01–0.03 J m⁻², yet their band edges shifted by up to 0.8 eV; simulations showed open-circuit voltage losses as large as 0.6 V.
watch_item: The conclusions rely on idealized first-principles surfaces and device simulations, so real devices may also be limited by defects, interface chemistry, and fabrication-driven facet distributions.
paper_title: Surface Physics of Low-Dimensional Pnictogen Chalcohalides and Its Impact on Photovoltaic Technologies
